title: human activities ignite most wildfires climate change is making them more 2026 08 06
text:
Human actions including arson and accidents ignite nine out of 10 wildfires in France, but a social media narrative that cites the statistic to downplay the effects of climate change is misleading.
France has experienced back-to-back heatwaves this summer and one of its worst wildfire seasons in recent years, with the area burned reaching 92,891 ​hectares (229,540 acres) so far – more than six times the average annual total between 2006 and 2025, according to the latest data from the European ‌Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS).
Responding to the devastating fires, some social media posts have cited a statistic on the French government's Georisques website, which says 90%
, opens new tab
 of forest fires are started by human activities – from discarded cigarette ends to barbecue accidents and arson. About a quarter of wildfires are ignited deliberately, it says.
One social media post
, opens new tab
 contrasted the data with what it called "the official line" that the climate is responsible. "The truth? ​9 out of 10 fires in France are caused by humans". Another post
, opens new tab
 quoted the same statistic to challenge media reports that "always blame the HEATWAVE for the fires".
But ​the claim that the statistic proves the limited role of climate factors in wildfires omits important context about the role of climate change ⁠in creating conditions favourable for more big, destructive fires.
The record-breaking late-June heatwave that hit France and other European countries would have been "virtually impossible" without human-caused ​climate change, according to a June 26 analysis
, opens new tab
 by the World Weather Attribution group of climate scientists.
Climate warming is making heatwaves hotter, which creates conditions
, opens new tab
 - including worsening drought that dries out vegetation - ​that allow fires started by humans or lightning to spread more rapidly.
A new analysis
, opens new tab
 using the Canadian Forest Service Fire Weather Index
, opens new tab
 (FWI), which combines temperature, precipitation, wind and fuel moisture - all influenced in part by climate warming - found that the number of summer days featuring extreme fire-prone conditions in vast parts of the Iberian Peninsula, France, Italy, and Greece more than doubled between 1981 and 2025.
Raul Cordero, a climate ​scientist at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands and one of the study’s authors, said that while Europe has managed to reduce the number of fires over that ​period due to big strides in firefighting and prevention, the climate has become more conducive to extreme fires.
“We are increasingly moving toward a regime of fewer fires but potentially larger, faster and more ‌difficult-to-control events,” ⁠Cordero said.
In France, where this summer’s fires have forced more than 200,000 evacuations, EFFIS data
, opens new tab
 running back to 2006 shows recent seasons have seen some of the highest levels of fire activity.
According to a Reuters analysis of the data, which records fires affecting about 30 hectares or more, the average annual burned area between 2006 and 2015 was 3,444 hectares, rising to 26,068 hectares between 2016 and 2025.
Other factors that can exacerbate fire risk include shrinking populations in rural areas of some Mediterranean countries, leaving fewer people to clear vegetation ​to avoid fuel for forest fires building ​up.
However, the role of climate warming as ⁠a contributing factor is significant and can be measured.
In a 2025 modelling study
, opens new tab
, for example, researchers identified the "fingerprint" of longer-term climate warming in rising fire weather conditions over the last 50+ years in parts of the U.S. and Canada. They found that human-caused climate change ​accounted for at least 81% of the increase across the region, with some model estimates suggesting an even larger contribution during specific ​periods.
Higher night-time temperatures also ⁠mean conditions remain flammable, depriving firefighters of respite after dark.
A 2022 global study
, opens new tab
 based on satellite images of fires and land temperatures found that flammable conditions at night increased by an average 110 hours per year between 1979 and 2020, adding between one and 22 additional nights when flammability never ceases, depending on the region.
Climate change and changes in land use are expected to ⁠increase extreme ​fires globally by up to 14% by the end of the decade, the United Nations has warned
, opens new tab
, urging governments ​to invest more in prevention, rather than focusing mainly on responding after fires break out.
However, “we do not have an endless adaptation capacity", Cordero warned.
Misleading: The statistic that nine out of 10 wildfires are ignited by human activities ​does not negate the contribution of climate change creating conditions favourable for more big, destructive fires.
This article was produced by the Reuters Fact Check team. Read more about our fact-checking work.
